proposedTopics.title: Greedy
proposedTopics.description: Make the locally-optimal choice at each step and prove (or trust) it leads to a globally optimal result. Independent axis from DP — no overlapping-subproblem memoization needed.

proposedTopics.title: Interval scheduling
proposedTopics.description: Sort by end time, greedily keep an interval if it starts after the last kept interval ends. Recognize: "maximum number of non-overlapping intervals you can select".

proposedTopics.title: Jump game
proposedTopics.description: Track the farthest index reachable so far while scanning left to right; feasibility/min-jumps falls out of comparing current index to that frontier. Recognize: "can you reach the end", "minimum jumps to reach the end".

proposedTopics.title: Gas station
proposedTopics.description: If total gas >= total cost a solution exists; the starting point is right after the point where cumulative tank first goes negative. One greedy pass, no brute force needed. Recognize: circular-array feasibility with a running-total tell.

proposedTopics.title: Greedy + sorting
proposedTopics.description: Sort by the attribute that makes the greedy choice obvious (deadline, ratio, size), then make one linear pass assigning/selecting. Recognize: matching/assignment problems solvable by sorting one or two lists.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for the sort-by-end-time interval scheduling greedy? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: "maximum number of non-overlapping intervals", or the dual "fewest removals to make them non-overlapping". Sort by END, keep an interval iff it starts at-or-after the last kept end. Pitfall: sorting by start time instead — a long early-starting interval then blocks several short ones; and getting the touch case wrong (decide whether shared endpoints count as overlap). Related: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended is the same greedy with a per-day twist.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the interval-scheduling scan in your language of choice: given intervals, count the maximum number you can keep with no overlaps.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Sort intervals by end value. Track lastEnd = -infinity and a counter; for each interval, if its start >= lastEnd, take it (counter++, lastEnd = its end), else skip. Invariant: lastEnd is always the earliest possible end among all valid selections of the intervals seen so far, which leaves the most room for future picks.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Non-overlapping Intervals (Medium) — return the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest are non-overlapping.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Maximize kept intervals with the sort-by-end greedy, then removals = total - kept (overlap means start < lastEnd).

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for the farthest-reachable-frontier greedy? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: array of jump lengths, "can you reach the end" or "minimum jumps to reach the end" — a reachability question over indices. Maintain the farthest index reachable while scanning left to right. Pitfall: continuing to scan past an index the frontier can't reach (if i > farthest, you're stranded — return false); for min-jumps, incrementing the jump count per element instead of once per frontier boundary.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the reachability scan in your language of choice: given an array of max jump lengths, decide whether the last index is reachable from index 0.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: farthest = 0; scan i from 0: if i > farthest return false (stranded), else farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]); return true (or farthest >= last). Invariant: farthest is the maximum index reachable using only positions 0..i, so once i exceeds it no later position is reachable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Jump Game (Medium) — given max jump lengths, return whether you can reach the last index.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Track the farthest reachable index in one pass; you fail the instant the current index passes it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Jump Game II (Medium) — return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index (reachability guaranteed).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: BFS-by-levels on indices: bump the jump count only when the scan reaches the end of the current jump's range, resetting that boundary to the farthest seen.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for the running-total "start after the deficit" greedy? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: a circular array where you accumulate a resource and must find a feasible start index (gas minus cost per station). Feasibility test: total gas >= total cost. The answer is the index right after the point where the running tank first drops below zero. Pitfall: forgetting the total-sum feasibility check (returning a candidate start when no start works at all), or not resetting the tank to 0 when moving the candidate start. Related: Candy is a two-pass greedy variant on this leaf's spirit.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Gas Station (Medium) — find the starting station index from which you can complete the circular route once, or -1.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: If total(gas) < total(cost) return -1; otherwise a single valid start exists — it's one past wherever the running tank goes negative (reset the tank there).

proposedPrompts.promptText: When do you reach for "sort, then one greedy pass"? Name the problem-statement signals, and the classic pitfall.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Signals: matching/assignment problems where sorting one or both lists by the deciding attribute (size, deadline, ratio) makes the local choice obvious — pair the smallest that fits, or the extremes together. Pitfall: sorting by the wrong key, or an incorrect two-pointer advance (advancing the wrong pointer when no match is possible leaves a greedy that isn't optimal). Related: Task Scheduler is a greedy-framing problem carded under Heap / Priority Queue.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Assign Cookies (Easy) — maximize the number of children satisfied, giving each child at most one cookie of size >= that child's greed factor.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Sort both greed factors and cookie sizes; two pointers assign the smallest adequate cookie to the least-greedy unsatisfied child.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Solve: Boats to Save People (Medium) — fewest boats to carry everyone, each boat holding at most two people within a weight limit.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Sort weights; opposite-direction pointers pair the heaviest with the lightest when they fit together, otherwise send the heaviest alone.
